assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks reached 10^-18 fractional systematic uncertainty, a roughly hundredfold improvement over the cesium microwave standard. The magic-wavelength lattice idea (Katori) removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping a large atomic ensemble, which is an elegant and concrete measurement solution. It enables relativistic geodesy, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and a possible redefinition of the second. This is exactly the kind of instrument-driven advance that opens new ways of observing nature.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed and first demonstrated the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock; Ye's group (JILA) drove the strontium clock to the 10^-18 level and made the comparisons and ensemble/spectroscopy advances. Both credited names are well supported as a pair. The overlap with the earlier Hall/Hansch comb prize and with ion-clock work (Wineland, 2012) leaves some interpretive questions, but the pair is a clean configuration.
assessment.maturity: Mature: many independent groups (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, others) have reproduced and improved lattice clocks, and international comparisons and redefinition-of-the-second roadmaps are under way. Timing is good.
uncertainties: Whether clock credit should also include ion-clock or other lattice-clock contributors beyond the supplied names; I cannot verify exact priority details from memory.
The redefinition of the second is not yet decided, so the full practical impact is still partly prospective.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with laser-manipulated atoms gives inertial sensing, gravimetry, gradiometry, measurements of G and the fine structure constant, and tests of the equivalence principle. It translates a fundamental quantum phenomenon into a precision instrument. Realistic devices exist already, and gravimetry for geophysics and navigation are the type of application I follow closely.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard pioneered atom interferometers with gratings and light and the first atom interferometer; Bordé developed the theoretical framework and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer; Kasevich made the high-precision gravimeters, gradiometers and large-momentum-transfer devices. Chu (1997 cooling prize) and Ramsey/Hall overlap partly with this area, which complicates the allocation. The three-name set is plausible but Bordé versus others (e.g. Chu, Mlynek, Shimizu, Keith) is not entirely clear to me.
assessment.maturity: Mature in laboratory precision and commercial field instruments; fundamental tests are still improving and no single decisive discovery is yet reached. Recognition is reasonable but the strongest fundamental results may still lie ahead.
uncertainties: Overlap with prior prizes for laser cooling and with other early atom-interferometer groups makes the laureate set contestable.
Fundamental-physics headline results (equivalence principle at high precision) are not yet decisive.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed states of light beat the standard quantum limit in interferometry. Caves proposed the idea for gravitational-wave detectors, Kimble made the first squeezed-light demonstration, and squeezing is now routinely deployed in the LIGO, Virgo and GEO600 detectors, lifting sensitivity and detection rates. This is a convincing case of quantum optics applied as a measurement tool that opened a new way of observing nature.
assessment.attribution: Caves supplied the 1981 proposal; Kimble's group the first experimental squeezing (1986, with Slusher at Bell Labs as a parallel effort not in the supplied names); Schnabel and the GEO600 collaboration led deployment, while Mavalvala contributed to LIGO squeezing. With the supplied names, a fair trio is Caves, Kimble and Schnabel, but Slusher's priority is a concern and Mavalvala would be a defensible alternative.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by independent detectors and a clear sensitivity improvement, with quantum-enhanced operation standard in observing runs. Well matured, though the 2017 prize for LIGO already covers the detector itself.
uncertainties: Priority issues, notably Slusher and colleagues' first squeezing experiment, are outside the supplied names and I cannot verify these details independently.
Four credited names for a one-to-three prize is a tight fit and the relative roles of LIGO-side and GEO-side contributors are open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Individually trapped neutral atoms in optical tweezer arrays, entangled by Rydberg blockade, offer programmable quantum simulation and gates with hundreds of qubits. It gives direct, well characterised measurements of many-body quantum states and rapidly improving gate fidelities. The experimental progress is very concrete and has opened a new platform.
assessment.attribution: Saffman and Zoller-era proposals laid the Rydberg gate theory; Browaeys (and Grangier) demonstrated blockade between individual atoms, and Lukin's group scaled up programmable arrays and error-corrected logical-qubit experiments. Lukin appears under several candidates, which is not itself a merit concern but shows that the Lukin credit is spread over different achievements. The supplied trio is workable but not perfect; Jaksch, Cirac and Zoller proposals and the Birkl and Weiss arrays are outside the list.
assessment.maturity: Fast-moving. Replication across several groups and companies is strong, but the field's ultimate usefulness for computation is not established, so recognition is somewhat early.
uncertainties: Whether the prize is premature relative to fault-tolerant demonstrations.
Allocation of credit among tweezer-array pioneers and Rydberg-gate theorists is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond gave a room-temperature solid-state quantum sensor with nanoscale spatial resolution for magnetic field, electric field and temperature, with applications from condensed-matter imaging to biology. The coherence times, contrast and sensitivities are what matter experimentally, and these are well characterised.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup's group did the first optical detection of single NV spins (1997) and the early coherent control; Lukin and Walsworth developed the nanoscale magnetometry and sensing applications, with Walsworth also leading the ensemble and biological uses. I leave out the third name because the decisive early contributions look clearest for Wrachtrup, with Lukin as the leading sensing figure, but this is an imperfect fit and Awschalom, Jelezko and Hanson are outside the list.
assessment.maturity: Mature in the sense of broad, independent replication and commercial products; sensitivity records are still being improved and the biological applications remain developing.
uncertainties: Credit is distributed across many groups (Jelezko, Awschalom, Hanson, Yacoby, others) not in the supplied names.
Real-world impact beyond laboratory demonstrations is still partial.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The IceCube detector observed a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos and identified TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane as sources, giving a new observational window on cosmic-ray accelerators. It is a large and technically bold instrument that turned a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice into a telescope.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led IceCube; Spiering was a key figure in the AMANDA/IceCube and Baikal-era neutrino-telescope development. Credit for a project of this scale is spread over a large collaboration, and the Nobel recipients are plausibly the proponents, though the supplied names contain only two.
assessment.maturity: The discovery is confirmed by the detector data and by multimessenger follow-up, but source identification is still limited to a few objects, so the field is maturing rather than mature.
uncertainties: Large-collaboration attribution and the role of the earlier Baikal and AMANDA pioneers.
Number of identified sources is small, so the astrophysical interpretation is incomplete.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping, cooling and spectroscopy of antihydrogen and precision comparison of matter and antimatter (CPT tests, 1S-2S, hyperfine, gravity) are demanding experimental feats with clear fundamental motivation. The measurement precision keeps improving, and the techniques are impressive.
assessment.attribution: Gabrielse led the ATRAP effort and the precision antiproton and electron magnetic moment work; Hangst led ALPHA, which first trapped antihydrogen and later did spectroscopy. The pair is a plausible configuration, with other groups (ATHENA/ASACUSA, Hänsch-linked spectroscopy) outside the list.
assessment.maturity: Experiments are replicated by competing collaborations, but no symmetry violation has been found; recognition could be timely but the physical discovery is a null-result precision test rather than a discovery.
uncertainties: Absence of a violation lowers the discovery weight.
Credit among the several antihydrogen collaborations and the CERN antiproton decelerator builders is open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Event Horizon Telescope delivered the first horizon-scale images of M87* and Sgr A*, a spectacular measurement feat combining mm-wavelength VLBI, atomic-clock timing and global coordination. It tests strong-field gravity and accretion physics directly.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept, Doeleman led the EHT and the mm-VLBI development, and Moran contributed essential VLBI/SMA foundations. The EHT is a collaboration of several hundred people, and the supplied three-person set only partially captures the credit.
assessment.maturity: Two sources imaged with consistent ring structures, but polarisation and variability interpretations are still developing and gravity tests remain loose. Recognition is plausible, though the prize committee may feel the science case is still broadening.
uncertainties: Large-collaboration credit is difficult to divide among three persons.
Astrophysical interpretation (spin, jet launching) remains model-dependent.
